title: How The Iditarod Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race, the roughly 1,000-mile dog sled race across Alaska held since 1973. They cover the northern and southern routes, record finish times, the history of sled dogs (Siberian huskies, Alaskan malamutes, samoyeds, Alaskan huskies), their use in mail delivery, gold rush, Antarctic expeditions and wartime, and the origins of the race founded by Joe Reddington Sr. with Dorothy Page, including the common misconception that it commemorates the 1925 serum run to Nome. They describe sled team structure, dog care and diet, race qualification, prizes, the mushing gear, and the criticism of dog deaths, ulcers from drugs, culling of puppies at kennels, and animal welfare concerns. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about poop-themed movie names and a breastfeeding episode request, then a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and tour plug
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with a sponsor read for Squarespace, a spring tour plug for Seattle and Portland dates, and banter about Chuck's cold and the weather. They introduce the topic of the Iditarod.

segments.title: What the Iditarod is and its basic facts
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Iditarod as a grueling endurance dog sled race across cold Alaska terrain, held since 1973. They discuss temperatures, the northern and southern routes, checkpoints, and how race times have fallen from about twenty days to just over eight days.

segments.title: Mushing hardships and sled dog history
segments.summary: The hosts discuss sleep deprivation and hallucinations during the race, the word mush, and the origins of sled dogs in Alaska. They cover the breeds people assume pull sleds, the Alaskan husky, and dogs used for hauling and hunting by Inuit and Eskimo peoples.

segments.title: Sled dogs in history: mail, Antarctica, wars
segments.summary: The hosts describe dog mail delivery in Alaska until the airplane, dogs used in the gold rush, Arctic and Antarctic expeditions including the Japanese dogs Taro and Jiro, and use as war dogs in World War One and World War Two.
topics: Alaska mail delivery by dog sled

segments.title: Origins of the Iditarod and the serum run myth
segments.summary: Joe Reddington Sr. and Dorothy Page started the race to preserve the dog sled heritage as snowmobiles replaced sleds. The hosts correct the common belief that the race commemorates the 1925 serum run to Nome, explaining that the trail was used for a different purpose and that the Balto statue in New York reflects national attention.

segments.title: Ceremonial start, costs, and qualifying
segments.summary: The hosts explain the ceremonial kickoff in Anchorage and its move to Willow due to lack of snow, the costs of running a team and corporate sponsorship, and qualifying rules such as age eighteen and prior approved races.

segments.title: Sled team structure, dog selection, and training
segments.summary: The hosts describe the team: the musher, lead dogs, swing or point dogs, team dogs, and wheel dogs, plus the gang line and tug lines. They cover commands such as haw, gee, and whoa, selecting dogs for temperament and gait, and conditioning dogs from puppyhood.

segments.title: Dog diet, booties, musher gear, and prizes
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the high calorie diet for the dogs, food drops at checkpoints, booties, the musher's required gear and sled, running alongside the sled, and the prize money and awards including gold nuggets and Red Lantern.

segments.title: Dog deaths, drug use, culling, and animal welfare criticism
segments.summary: The hosts discuss dog deaths during the race and training, a 2009 incident where a dog suffocated at a checkpoint, ulcers from anti-inflammatory drugs, and criticism from animal welfare groups. They also cover kennel culling of puppies and the hosts' personal opinions on the race.
